levels.title: SQL 1 · Clean Syntax & Formatting Basics
levels.concept_capsule: Readable SQL puts every major clause on its own line, uppercases reserved keywords, and opens with a one-line intent comment so BI reviews and audits take seconds.
levels.starter_code: select id,email from users where active=1 order by id desc
levels.reference_solution:
-- Fetch active user accounts ordered by latest ID
SELECT
  id,
  email
FROM users
WHERE active = 1
ORDER BY id DESC;

keywords_glossary.role: Declares the exact columns to project. In production, avoiding `SELECT *` prevents broken downstream reports and unnecessary network I/O.
Specifies the source table or view. In production, explicit table references make ETL lineage easy to trace.
Filters rows before sorting or returning results. In production, it trims disk scans and keeps inactive records out of dashboards.
Sorts output deterministically from highest to lowest. In production, explicit ordering keeps paginated views and daily snapshots consistent.

formatting_mechanics.indentation: Indent projected columns by 2 spaces under SELECT so the projection block stands out visually.
formatting_mechanics.line_breaks: Start SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and ORDER BY on separate lines and place one column per line.
formatting_mechanics.punctuation: Separate columns with trailing commas (no comma on the last column), add spaces around `=`, and terminate with `;`.
formatting_mechanics.documentation_standard: Lead with a single `-- ` comment describing the business question the query answers.

analogous_example.title: Available products sorted by price
analogous_example.code:
-- Fetch in-stock products ordered from highest to lowest price
SELECT
  sku,
  unit_price
FROM products
WHERE in_stock = 1
ORDER BY unit_price DESC;
analogous_example.why_it_works: Keywords are uppercase on left-aligned clause lines, columns use 2-space indentation, and the header comment documents intent on a separate domain.

levels.title: SQL 2 · Edge Cases & Documentation
levels.concept_capsule: When joining tables with aggregates, `LEFT JOIN` preserves unmatched rows, explicit `AS` aliases stabilize output contracts, and `GROUP BY` defines exact reporting granularity.
levels.starter_code: select u.id,count(o.id) from users u left join orders o on u.id=o.user_id group by u.id
levels.reference_solution:
-- Count orders per user including users with zero orders
SELECT
  u.id,
  COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON u.id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.id;

keywords_glossary.role: Keeps every row from the left table even when no match exists on the right. In production, it prevents dropping zero-activity entities from coverage KPIs.
keywords_glossary.example_inline: LEFT JOIN employees AS e ON d.id = e.dept_id

keywords_glossary.role: Counts non-null values and assigns a clear column name via `AS`. In production, it avoids anonymous headers that break BI models and API consumers.
Groups rows by every non-aggregated column in `SELECT`. In production, this ensures strict ANSI SQL compliance across engines.

formatting_mechanics.indentation: Indent projected columns and the `ON` join predicate by 2 spaces under their parent clauses.
formatting_mechanics.line_breaks: Put `LEFT JOIN` on its own line and move `ON` to the next indented line.
formatting_mechanics.punctuation: Use explicit `AS` for both table and column aliases, space around `=`, and close with `;`.
formatting_mechanics.documentation_standard: State in the leading `-- ` comment what is counted and that zero-match entities are preserved.

analogous_example.title: Employee headcount per department including empty ones
analogous_example.code:
-- Count employees per department including departments with zero staff
SELECT
  d.id,
  COUNT(e.id) AS headcount
FROM departments AS d
LEFT JOIN employees AS e
  ON d.id = e.dept_id
GROUP BY d.id;
analogous_example.why_it_works: It separates `LEFT JOIN` and `ON`, aliases tables and aggregates explicitly with `AS`, and uses `COUNT(e.id)` so unmatched departments return 0.
